title: Female choice over many generations can produce male ornaments

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Female choice over many generations can produce male ornaments

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Female birds, by choosing the most melodious or beautiful males over thousands of generations, can produce a marked change in male song or plumage.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I can see no good reason to doubt that female birds, by selecting, during thousands of generations, the most melodious or beautiful males, according to their standard of beauty, might produce a marked effect.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IV, “Natural Selection”; section “Sexual Selection”. Scope: birds, especially species with male display

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch04-07: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.61

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The component predictions are measurable and existing studies can establish the mechanism in particular birds. Public data rarely contain preference, inheritance and multigenerational response together.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Combine female mate-choice measurements, male song or plumage phenotypes, reproductive success and pedigree or genomic heritability. A heritable ornament preferred by females and associated with higher mating success supports cumulative female-choice evolution; alternative ecological or male-competition effects must be controlled.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Long-term historical causation cannot be observed directly.

Female choice, male competition and ecological selection often covary.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.43
data existence: 0.62
analysis feasibility: 0.59
operationalizability: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.59

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Short-term genetic covariances and phylogenetic associations are available as proxies, and they can show that preference is capable of shifting male traits in particular species. They do not replay the historical, multi-thousand-generation process, and a negative result in one clade would leave the possibility claim standing. Existing public data therefore test a restricted, present-day proxy and do not separate female choice from other sexual selection.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate the genetic covariance between female preference and male song or plumage, and test whether ornament elaboration increases with preference along bird phylogenies. A positive evolutionary response to preference would support the capacity. The wording is a possibility over thousands of generations, so failure in studied species would not refute it, and male-male competition predicts the same ornaments.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Female preference time series over many generations do not exist.

Male-male competition and female choice produce overlapping ornament patterns.

Song archives and morphological averages omit the preference-trait covariance.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.46
data existence: 0.52
operationalizability: 0.46
discriminating power: 0.4
